chunks.text: Cassia fistula belongs to the pea family Fabaceae (subfamily Caesalpinioideae) and is also known as Indian laburnum, purging cassia, or pudding-pipe tree, with older synonyms including Cathartocarpus fistula. It is native to the Indian subcontinent and adjacent Southeast Asia and is now a widely planted ornamental across the tropics and subtropics, from India to Thailand, Laos and Sri Lanka. It is a medium-sized tree, 10–20 m tall, with deciduous pinnate leaves 15–60 cm long made up of three to eight pairs of leaflets, and its signature feature: brilliant yellow, five-petalled flowers 4–7 cm across, hanging in pendulous racemes 20–40 cm long that can nearly obscure the foliage during peak bloom in the hot, dry pre-monsoon season. Long (30–60 cm) cylindrical pods with a distinctive pungent-smelling pulp follow the flowers, and the heartwood is noted for exceptional durability, historically used in construction.

In Ayurveda the tree is called 'aragvadha', meaning 'disease killer', and its fruit pulp is a traditional purgative, still sold commercially in some herbal laxative preparations — though Ayurvedic sources themselves caution against self-medication without supervision. Ecologically the tree is not a nitrogen fixer, unlike many other legumes; carpenter bees and various butterflies pollinate its flowers, and historical records note golden jackals eating and dispersing its fruit.

Cassia fistula is Thailand's national tree and national flower, called 'ratchaphruek', where its gold blossoms symbolise Thai royalty (celebrated in the 2006–2007 Royal Flora Ratchaphruek festival). In India it is the state flower of Kerala, known locally as 'kani konna', and its blooms are central to the Vishu festival each April; the tree has also appeared on an Indian commemorative postage stamp. In Sri Lanka it is commonly grown in Buddhist temples under the Sinhala name 'Ehela' and is the provincial tree of the North Central Province, while in Laos it is called 'dok khoun' and its flowering coincides with Lao New Year, when the blooms are used as temple offerings symbolising prosperity.
